content: Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR or S/N) is a concept originating in electrical engineering but is also widely applied in other fields such as scientific measurements, biological cell signaling, and oral lore. It is defined as the ratio of the power of a signal to the power of the noise that corrupts the signal. In simpler terms, SNR compares the level of a desired signal (e.g., music) to the level of background noise. A higher SNR indicates that the background noise is less intrusive. Technical Definition In engineering, the signal-to-noise ratio is the power ratio between a meaningful signal and the background noise. Mathematically, it is expressed as: [ text{SNR} = frac{P_{text{signal}}}{P_{text{noise}}} = left( frac{A_{text{signal}}}{A_{text{noise}}} right)^2 ] Here, (P) represents the average power, and (A) is the root mean square (RMS) amplitude. Both the signal and noise power (or amplitude) must be measured at equivalent points in the system and within the same system bandwidth. Since many signals have a wide dynamic range, SNR is often expressed in decibels (dB) using a logarithmic scale. In decibels, SNR is defined as: [ text{SNR (dB)} = 10 log_{10} left( frac{P_{text{signal}}}{P_{text{noise}}} right) = 20 log_{10} left( frac{A_{text{signal}}}{A_{text{noise}}} right) ] If the signal and noise are measured across the same impedance, the SNR can be calculated using the amplitude ratio. Electrical SNR and Acoustics SNR is often used to compare electromagnetic signals, but it can also be applied to sound stimuli. Due to the definition of decibels, the SNR calculation remains consistent regardless of the type of signal being evaluated, such as power, current, or voltage. SNR is closely related to the concept of dynamic range, which measures the ratio between noise and the maximum undistorted signal on a channel. While dynamic range focuses on the strongest possible signal, SNR measures the ratio between noise and an arbitrary signal on the channel. This requires selecting a representative or reference signal for measurement. SNR typically represents an average value, as instantaneous SNR values can vary significantly. Conceptually, SNR normalizes the noise level to 1 (0 dB) and measures how much the signal stands out. A higher SNR generally indicates a cleaner signal. Image Processing and Interferometry In image processing, SNR is defined as the ratio of the mean pixel value to the standard deviation of pixel values. Related metrics include contrast ratio and contrast-to-noise ratio. In imaging systems, the relationship between optical power and voltage is linear, so the SNR of the electrical signal is calculated using the 10-log rule. In interferometric systems, where the signal of interest comes from one arm of the interferometer, the electromagnetic wave's field is proportional to the voltage. Assuming the intensity in the reference arm is constant, the optical power of the measurement arm is directly proportional to the electrical power. In such cases, the SNR follows the 20-log rule. The Rose criterion, named after Albert Rose, states that an SNR of at least 5 is required to distinguish image features with 100% certainty. An SNR below 5 results in less than 100% certainty in identifying image details. Measurement Devices Measurement devices are often affected by parasitic phenomena, including electronic noise, wind, vibrations, gravitational effects, temperature variations, and humidity changes. These disturbances depend on the measured phenomenon and the device's sensitivity. Noise can sometimes be reduced by controlling the environment. Alternatively, if the noise characteristics are known and differ from the signal, it is possible to filter or process the signal to enhance the SNR. When noise is random and the signal is constant, increasing the measurement time can improve the SNR. In Fourier transform analysis, random noise corresponds to high frequencies, while broad signal peaks correspond to low frequencies. The highest frequency can be estimated as the inverse of the peak width. Digital Signals In digital systems, the number of bits used to store each value determines the maximum SNR. In this context, noise arises from quantization errors during analog-to-digital conversion. The noise level is non-linear and signal-dependent, with different calculations for various signal models. Noise is modeled as an analog error signal added to the signal before quantization (additive noise). The modulation error ratio (MER) is a measure of SNR in digitally modulated signals and can also be expressed in decibels. Fixed-Point Systems For n-bit integers with uniform quantization levels, the dynamic range (DR) is determined. Assuming a uniform distribution of input signal values, quantization noise is a uniformly distributed random signal with a peak-to-peak amplitude of one quantization level. This relationship explains statements like 16-bit audio has a dynamic range of 96 dB. Each additional quantization bit increases the dynamic range by approximately 6 dB. For a full-scale sine wave signal, quantization noise approximates a sawtooth wave with a peak-to-peak amplitude of one quantization level. Floating-Point Systems Floating-point numbers allow a trade-off between SNR and dynamic range. While floating-point systems offer a much larger dynamic range than fixed-point systems, they do so at the cost of a lower SNR. This makes floating-point systems preferable in scenarios with large or unpredictable dynamic ranges. However, the large dynamic range of floating-point systems requires careful algorithm design. Notes Analog-to-digital converters have additional noise sources that reduce the SNR compared to the theoretical maximum from idealized quantization noise. Special filters, such as DIN-A, DIN-B, DIN-C, DIN-D, CCIR-601, and video comb filters, are often used to weight noise. The maximum possible full-scale signal can be measured as peak-to-peak or RMS. Audio systems use RMS, while video systems use peak-to-peak, resulting in a 9 dB higher SNR for video. In digital systems, SNR is often expressed using (E_b/N_0), the energy per bit per noise power spectral density. Informal Use Informally, signal-to-noise ratio refers to the ratio of useful information to irrelevant or false data. In online forums, off-topic posts and spam are considered noise that interferes with the signal of meaningful discussion. For example, in Bugzilla, comments like please fix this clutter the discussion without contributing to solving the issue. Moderation systems can improve the SNR by filtering out irrelevant posts. Similarly, the wiki collaboration model addresses this problem by allowing users to moderate content, ideally adding signal while removing noise.
